abstract: Humans are remarkably efficient at learning from limited experience because they can generalize quickly. Doing so, however, requires first learning about the latent structures that govern outcomes. The dominant theoretical framework to understand this interactive cycle between learning task representations and generalisation is deep learning, which updates parameters throughout multi-layered neural networks using deep credit assignment. Yet, whether the brain uses a similar "deep" approach to learning is unclear. Here, we derive and test a prediction that uniquely characterizes deep credit assignment, namely, that a single learning experience should trigger immediate, structured representation changes that are non-local (i.e. generalize beyond the observed experience), and adapt as learning proceeds. Using fMRI (N=51) and neural network simulations, we tested whether feedback on a limited set of items induces structured changes in the representations of other, non-feedbacked items during a partially-observable reinforcement learning task. We find that with sufficient learning, feedback on a small set of trials begins to induce rapid, context-dependent shifts in non-local orbitofrontal cortex representations that extend beyond experienced items and predict concurrent improvements in behavioral generalization. The neural findings and their link to behaviour were mirrored by representation learning dynamics in performance-matched recurrent neural networks, trained using gradient descent on the same curricula as participants. These findings reveal fast, non-local dynamics of representation learning that support generalization and are shared across humans and distributed deep networks.
